forming.name: Forming
forming.blurb: Stamping, roll forming, hot stamping, springback

welding.name: Welding
welding.blurb: Laser welding, spot welding, joining challenges

questions.question: Which process best suits AHSS grades with low total elongation, like martensitic steel?
questions.explanation: Roll forming bends the strip incrementally through paired roller dies, which minimises strain localisation and compensates springback, so it handles grades that would crack in a draw die.

questions.question: For the same part shape and thickness, springback in AHSS compared with mild steel is:
questions.explanation: Springback scales with the as-formed flow stress, and AHSS starts higher and work hardens more, so the elastic energy stored in the part is larger.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the three shapes springback takes?
questions.explanation: Springback shows up as angular change, sidewall curl and twist. Grain growth is a thermal effect, not an elastic recovery one.

questions.question: Why do AHSS parts need higher press loads than mild steel?
questions.explanation: It is strength, not thickness. Higher yield strength plus rapid work hardening raises the force needed at every stage of the stroke.

questions.question: What is the main job of a draw bead?
questions.explanation: Draw beads control how fast metal feeds in from the binder, and the strain they add also reduces the elastic recovery that causes springback.

questions.question: Any mechanical cutting operation does what to the ductility of the cut edge?
questions.explanation: Blanking, piercing, shearing and trimming all leave a heavily work hardened zone with a reduced n-value, which is why edges fail below the forming limit curve.

questions.question: Which standard covers the hole expansion test?
questions.explanation: ISO 16630 is the hole expansion test and VDA 238-100 the bend test. They are two of the few standardised ways to characterise local formability.

questions.question: Press hardening steels are heated to roughly what temperature for full austenitisation?
questions.explanation: Around 900 C, held in a roller hearth furnace over 30 m long. Heating that much steel is why a hot stamping line often draws more than 2 MW.

questions.question: Which press can dwell at bottom dead centre to reduce springback?
questions.explanation: A servo press has programmable slide motion, so it can slow the draw, dwell or re-strike at bottom dead centre, none of which a flywheel press can do.

questions.question: Why should re-forming operations be avoided on press hardened parts?
questions.explanation: After quenching the part is fully martensitic and extremely strong, so any further forming needs loads the tooling was never designed for.

questions.question: What is the critical cooling rate for 22MnB5 press hardening steel?
questions.explanation: Below 27 C/s the austenite transforms to something other than martensite, so any zone quenched slower than this misses its strength target.

questions.question: Roll forming ultra high-strength steel needs how many passes compared with mild steel?
questions.explanation: Roughly 50 percent more stands, with the overbend spread evenly from pass to pass rather than loaded into the last one.

questions.question: A 600 ton mechanical press about 3 inches off bottom dead centre can deliver roughly:
questions.explanation: De-rated tonnage. The full rating only exists near bottom dead centre, which is why embossments engaging off bottom catch people out.

questions.question: In a structural stamping, which phase dominates total force and energy?
questions.explanation: Embossing dominates both, even though its punch travel is a small fraction of the draw depth.

questions.question: Forming a hat cross member in DP 350/600 takes how much energy versus mild steel?
questions.explanation: About twice the energy for the same geometry, which is a press selection issue rather than a tooling one.

questions.question: In roll forming, tolerances get hard to hold on radii larger than:
questions.explanation: Springback rises with both strength and bend radius, so large radii lose dimensional control. Using the minimum allowable radius is the usual fix.

questions.question: How far into the sheet does the work hardened zone from a cut edge typically extend?
questions.explanation: About half the metal thickness in from the cut. That band of reduced n-value is what makes edges split before the forming limit curve says they should.

questions.question: Which press hardening route avoids liquid metal embrittlement with zinc coatings?
questions.explanation: The indirect route forms the shape cold, then heats and quenches in the tool, so there is no liquid zinc present while the steel is being deformed.

questions.question: Optimised cutting parameters improved hole expansion ratio by roughly how much?
questions.explanation: Around 60 percent, with shearing force also dropping by more than half, which eases snap-through and extends tool life.

questions.question: Typical hardness of a 1500 MPa class press hardened part after quenching?
questions.explanation: Roughly 470 to 510 HV, alongside 950 to 1200 MPa yield and 1300 to 1700 MPa tensile strength.

questions.question: LME cracking needs liquid zinc, a susceptible microstructure, and what third factor?
questions.explanation: All three have to be present at once. Remove any single one and the crack does not form.

questions.question: Typical weld time for a resistance spot weld in steel?
questions.explanation: Roughly a fifth of a second. The nugget forms fast because contact resistance heats the joint faster as it gets hotter.

questions.question: Typical current range used in resistance spot welding?
questions.explanation: Far higher than arc welding, because the heat comes from resistance across a joint held for only a fraction of a second.

questions.question: Most common way to join sheets into a tailor welded blank?
questions.explanation: Laser welding dominates. Mash seam welding is possible but needs an overlap, which adds mass, and leaves a much larger heat affected zone.

questions.question: Compared with mild steel, laser welding AHSS needs clamping forces that are:
questions.explanation: Higher, because springback and part distortion make good fit-up harder to achieve and hold.

questions.question: In spot welding, where does the heat that starts the nugget come from?
questions.explanation: Resistance at the sheet-to-sheet contact. Steel resists far more than the copper electrodes, so the steel heats while the electrodes stay cool.

questions.question: Common minimum button diameter rule for an acceptable spot weld?
questions.explanation: Four times the square root of sheet thickness is the usual automotive and steel industry benchmark for minimum button size.

questions.question: A laser lap weld typically penetrates how far into the bottom sheet?
questions.explanation: About half way, unless the design calls for an edge weld instead. Lap joints also give a wider process window than butt joints.

questions.question: Compared with a laser weld, the heat affected zone of a mash seam weld is:
questions.explanation: Considerably larger. The peak temperature is lower, which can help formability, but the wide HAZ and thicker joint usually cancel that out.

questions.question: Which change widens the usable current range in spot welding AHSS?
questions.explanation: More electrode force, and more weld time, both open the process window. AHSS starts with a narrower window than mild steel.

questions.question: Recommended sheet gap for laser lap welding of zinc-coated AHSS?
questions.explanation: A small intermittent gap gives vaporised zinc a route out instead of trapping it in the melt. Too large and the top surface underfills.

questions.question: How much does the weld current range grow per extra 500 N of electrode force?
questions.explanation: Around 500 A on average across AHSS from 600 to 1400 MPa. It is the cheapest way to buy back process window.

questions.question: How much does the weld current range grow per extra 40 ms of weld time?
questions.explanation: Around 250 A. Weld time and electrode force are the two levers that widen an AHSS weld lobe.

questions.question: Fit-up gap guideline for a laser butt weld, as a share of the thinnest sheet?
questions.explanation: 3 to 10 percent of the thinnest sheet for the gap, and 5 to 12 percent for offset. Edge quality matters as much as the numbers.

questions.question: The usable weld current range runs from minimum button size up to what?
questions.explanation: The upper bound is the current at which molten metal expels. The gap between that and minimum button size is the whole process window.

questions.question: How can zinc-coated sheets be laser lap welded with no gap at all?
questions.explanation: Two beams: the first evaporates the zinc, the second makes the weld. It removes the gap requirement rather than working around it.

questions.question: What degrades the spot weldability of TRIP steels relative to DP?
questions.explanation: The alloy additions TRIP needs for retained austenite hurt weldability. Pulsation or dilution welding schedules recover it.

questions.question: A pulsation welding schedule typically uses how many pulses?
questions.explanation: Two to four, with controlled cool time between them, giving much better command of heat input and nugget growth.

questions.question: Compared with mild steel, the weld lobe for AHSS is:
questions.explanation: Tighter, and shifted toward lower currents. A smaller window is why weld size checks need to be more frequent.

questions.question: What does an insufficient electrode hold time do when welding zinc-coated AHSS?
questions.explanation: It leaves liquid zinc on the surface and lets thermal stress build after the caps lift. Hold time alone can decide cracked versus crack-free.

questions.question: Typical average iron content in a galvannealed coating?
questions.explanation: Zinc and steel inter-diffuse into an iron-zinc alloy averaging 8 to 12 percent iron, and that iron is what makes galvanneal weld well.

questions.question: How does a zinc coating protect steel at a scratch?
questions.explanation: Zinc acts as a sacrificial anode and corrodes preferentially, so bare steel exposed by a scratch or stone chip stays protected.

questions.question: Which coating is essentially pure zinc?
questions.explanation: GI is free zinc. Aluminium in the bath forms a thin Fe2Al5 barrier that stops iron diffusing up into the coating.

questions.question: The white corrosion product on galvanized steel is mainly:
questions.explanation: Zinc carbonate and zinc hydroxide. It signals the coating doing its job, not the steel underneath failing.

questions.question: Aluminized coatings are preferred where the part sees:
questions.explanation: Aluminium melts far above zinc, so aluminized sheet suits engine compartment and exhaust applications where zinc would not survive.

questions.question: Typical coating weight for hot dip galvanized or electrogalvanized sheet?
questions.explanation: 50 to 60 g/m2 is the usual range, against 30 to 45 for galvanneal, which is kept lighter to limit powdering.

questions.question: Why is hot dip galvanizing economical for sheet steel?
questions.explanation: Cold rolled steel can be annealed and coated in the same continuous operation, so corrosion protection adds one line rather than two.

questions.question: A reddish tinge in the corrosion product of galvanneal indicates:
questions.explanation: It comes from the iron alloyed into the coating and should not be read as corrosion of the steel underneath.

questions.question: Which coating offers no cathodic protection to the steel?
questions.explanation: Aluminium based coatings work as a barrier through a surface oxide layer, but unlike zinc they do not sacrifice themselves to protect exposed steel.

questions.question: An uncoated blank in the austenitising furnace develops what problem?
questions.explanation: Scale, which blocks heat transfer during quenching, damages tool surfaces when it flakes, and has to be shot blasted off afterwards.

questions.question: Why are galvanneal coatings usually run at 30 to 45 g/m2?
questions.explanation: The hard iron-zinc alloy powders against tooling, worst of all through draw beads. Thinner coatings limit how much comes off.

questions.question: What creates the thin Fe2Al5 barrier layer in a galvanized coating?
questions.explanation: Small aluminium additions to the molten zinc. Drop the aluminium and you lose the barrier, which is exactly how galvanneal is made.

questions.question: Iron content across a galvanneal coating runs roughly from surface to interface as:
questions.explanation: About 5 percent at the tool-contacting surface rising to as much as 25 percent at the steel interface, set by bath chemistry and time at temperature.

questions.question: Which coating typically shows the highest coefficient of friction in forming?
questions.explanation: Galvanneal sits highest, electrogalvanized in the middle, hot dip galvanized lowest. Coating choice is a friction decision as much as a corrosion one.

questions.question: Why do electrogalvanized surfaces hold lubricant well despite high dry friction?
questions.explanation: The stacked plate-like morphology traps and holds lubricant, which smoother hot dipped surfaces cannot do as effectively.

questions.question: Furnace scale on an uncoated hot stamping blank causes what during quenching?
questions.explanation: Scale insulates the part from the tool, and may stop the critical cooling rate being reached at all.

questions.question: Aluminium-silicon coated press hardening steel is limited to which route?
questions.explanation: Direct only. The coating cracks if the blank is cold formed first, and it needs enough furnace time to alloy with the base steel.

questions.question: What production benefit does the iron in a galvanneal coating deliver?
questions.explanation: Weldability. It is the reason many body shops prefer galvanneal over free zinc despite the powdering trade-off.

questions.question: Which coating has no alloy phase variation to manage across production lines?
questions.explanation: Electrogalvanized coatings are uniform in composition, unlike galvanneal, whose several phases can differ line to line and change forming and painting behaviour.

questions.question: One drawback of aluminium-silicon coating in a roller hearth furnace is that it:
questions.explanation: Coating pickup on the rollers drives up furnace maintenance cost, and the coating is abrasive on tooling as well.

questions.question: At what speed does Bharat NCAP run its frontal offset deformable barrier test?
questions.explanation: 64 kmph into an offset deformable barrier, the same frontal speed Global NCAP and Euro NCAP use, so results are broadly comparable.

questions.question: Which vehicles does Bharat NCAP currently assess?
questions.explanation: M1 passenger cars up to eight seats and a gross vehicle weight of 3500 kg. Participation is voluntary, not mandatory.

questions.question: Bharat NCAP publishes star ratings for which two groups?
questions.explanation: Adult occupant protection and child occupant protection are scored and starred separately, so a car can rate well for one and poorly for the other.

questions.question: What is a crumple zone actually doing in a frontal impact?
questions.explanation: It converts kinetic energy into plastic deformation and stretches the stopping distance, which lowers the deceleration the occupants feel.

questions.question: Which part of the body structure is designed NOT to deform?
questions.explanation: The safety cage has to hold its shape so survival space and door openings survive. Everything ahead of and beside it is designed to collapse in a controlled way.

questions.question: Electronic Stability Control mainly prevents what?
questions.explanation: It brakes individual wheels to keep the car on the driver's intended path. NCAP programmes treat it as a baseline safety assist, not an optional extra.

questions.question: How many stages of safety does the Euro NCAP 2026 protocol assess?
questions.explanation: Safe driving, crash avoidance, crash protection and post-crash safety, each scored out of 100. It is the biggest rewrite since the star system arrived in 2009.

questions.question: Where is the battery pack mounted in most modern electric cars?
questions.explanation: A flat pack in the floor keeps the centre of gravity low, but it also puts the most expensive and most fire-sensitive component right in the side impact zone.

questions.question: The FutureSteelVehicle body structure was how much lighter than its benchmark?
questions.explanation: 35 percent, an 188 kg structure, achieved with no cost penalty for the mass saved.

questions.question: What does the Steel E-Motive body structure weigh?
questions.explanation: 282 kg against a 374 kg reference, on a body designed around a battery instead of an engine.

questions.question: Bharat NCAP runs its mobile deformable barrier side impact test at:
questions.explanation: 50 kmph for the moving deformable barrier. The pole side impact is a separate, slower but far more concentrated test.

questions.question: At what speed is the Bharat NCAP pole side impact conducted?
questions.explanation: 29 kmph, but into a narrow rigid pole. The low speed is deceptive: all the energy goes through a very small area of the side structure.

questions.question: How many adult occupant protection points does a five-star Bharat NCAP rating need?
questions.explanation: 27 out of 32 for adult occupant protection. Three stars needs 16, so the gap between three and five stars is where most structural work sits.

questions.question: A five-star Bharat NCAP child occupant protection rating needs how many points?
questions.explanation: 41 points. Child protection is scored on its own scale, which is why the two star ratings on a Bharat NCAP certificate often differ.

questions.question: When did Bharat NCAP testing formally begin?
questions.explanation: 1 October 2023, under AIS-197, drawing on Global NCAP's protocols. Version 2.0, adding a full-width frontal test, is slated for 2027.

questions.question: Which assessment area is new in the Euro NCAP 2026 protocol?
questions.explanation: Post-crash safety became its own scored category, covering rescue information, extrication and what happens in the minutes after the impact.

questions.question: What does Euro NCAP 2026 require of an electric vehicle after a crash?
questions.explanation: High-voltage isolation, plus electric door handles that still work so rescuers can open the doors, and a warning to occupants about battery fire risk.

questions.question: Why must a front rail crush axially rather than fold sideways?
questions.explanation: Progressive axial folding absorbs far more energy per unit mass than a bending collapse, which is why trigger dents and section design matter so much.

questions.question: Why do TRIP steels suit crush zone parts?
questions.explanation: Retained austenite left after forming transforms to martensite during the crash, so the part strain hardens exactly when the energy needs absorbing.

questions.question: Why do battery electric vehicles use deep multi-cell rocker sections?
questions.explanation: The rocker is the last structure between a pole and the battery, so it has to stop intrusion in a very short crush distance rather than simply absorb energy.

questions.question: The 1998 ULSAB body-in-white cut body structure weight by how much?
questions.explanation: 25 percent at no cost penalty. Building real hardware, not just a model, is what made the industry take it seriously.

questions.question: In which year did the ULSAB programme begin?
questions.explanation: 1994, when a consortium of 35 sheet steel producers from 22 countries set out to design a lightweight steel body.

questions.question: How many times can steel be recycled without losing quality?
questions.explanation: Steel is one of the few materials that keeps its properties through recycling, so a can can become a bridge, a ship or a car.

questions.question: Steel and iron make up roughly what share of an average vehicle by weight?
questions.explanation: About 65 percent, which is why end-of-life vehicles are worth shredding and why cars are the most recycled consumer product.

questions.question: The average recycling rate for steel and iron in cars is about:
questions.explanation: Around 90 percent. Magnetic separation makes steel trivially easy to pull out of a shredded vehicle.

questions.question: Which programme in the UltraLight family covered closures?
questions.explanation: ULSAC took on doors and other closures, showing lightweight steel solutions that were still manufacturable and affordable.

questions.question: What did the ULSAS programme study?
questions.explanation: Suspensions. In 2001 it matched the mass of an aluminium system while costing 30 percent less.

questions.question: Roughly how much steel is recycled from end-of-life vehicles each year?
questions.explanation: More than 14 million tons, equivalent to about 13.5 million cars.

questions.question: TWIP steels belong to which generation of AHSS?
questions.explanation: Second generation. First generation covers DP, TRIP, CP, MS and PHS, and third generation began commercialising around 2020.

questions.question: Which of these is a first generation AHSS?
questions.explanation: Dual phase, along with TRIP, complex phase, martensitic and press hardening steels. TWIP is second generation, medium Mn is third.

questions.question: AHSS are multiphase steels with a minimum specified tensile strength of at least:
questions.explanation: 440 MPa, together with a multiphase microstructure. The 980 MPa figure is only one informal threshold for calling a steel ultra high strength.

questions.question: Global commercialisation of third generation AHSS started around:
questions.explanation: Around 2020. These grades are engineered for formability measured in tensile, sheared edge and bending tests, not tensile numbers alone.

questions.question: Medium manganese steels contain roughly what manganese content?
questions.explanation: Around 3 to 12 percent, enough to keep austenite stable at room temperature so the TRIP effect works during stamping.

questions.question: TRIP steels sustain an n-value of roughly what through deformation?
questions.explanation: 0.23 to 0.25, held throughout deformation as retained austenite keeps transforming, rather than fading after a few percent strain.

questions.question: At equal tensile strength above 800 MPa, complex phase yield strength versus dual phase is:
questions.explanation: Higher, because carbo-nitride precipitation strengthens the ferrite. CP also bends and stretches cut edges better than DP.

questions.question: The bake hardening increase in a dual phase steel is typically:
questions.explanation: More than 100 MPa on top of the work hardening from forming, provided the part saw enough forming strain to start with.

questions.question: Dual phase steels show their highest work hardening rate at what strain?
questions.explanation: In the first few percent, which happens to be the strain range of outer panel stamping. After that the n-value falls toward HSLA levels.

questions.question: How many steel producers formed the original ULSAB consortium?
questions.explanation: 35 producers from 22 countries, and every finding was released into the public domain free of charge.

questions.question: ULSAS matched the mass of an aluminium suspension while delivering what cost benefit?
questions.explanation: A 30 percent cost advantage at equal mass, which is the argument steel has made in every programme since.

questions.question: Which phase is associated with better sheared edge ductility?
questions.explanation: Bainite. Accelerated cooling on the hot mill run-out table is how ferrite-bainite grades are produced for edge-critical parts.
